To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
end-of-life decisions are taken in different ways depending on the place of death.
the place of death is associated with the type of end-of-life decisions taken, and that the place of decision-making is related with the place of death, especially in Belgium, Switzerland and Sweden.

The incidence of end-of-life decision making varies by place of death; end-of-life decisionmaking is more likely to be discussed with patients in their own home, and with other caregivers in care homes; end-of-life decisions are taken more often in hospitals and care homes, but are relatively more likely to be taken at home.
In summary, our research is concerned with
end-of-life decision making and communication in Belgium, Denmark and Sweden, and with end-of-life communication in Switzerland.
the end-of-life decisions made for patients who die in a hospital, at home or in a care institution.
the end-of-life care of patients in the last 3 months of their life, in particular with the end-of life decision-making and the place where people die.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the place of death is a significant factor in end-of-life decisions and communication.
the incidence of end-of-life decisions varies by place of death and that end-of-life decisions are generally less frequently discussed in the home environment.
the place where people die is associated with the end-of-life decisions taken, the communication surrounding those decisions, and the way of dying, but that the differences are relatively small.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the place of death is related to the end-of-life decisions that are made, and that end-of-life communication differs between the settings.
the place of death seems to be related to the type of end-of-life decisions taken.
the place of death makes a difference in the end-of-life care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
end-of-life care decisions are made at home more than in the hospital, and that the decision to withhold treatment is made in the hospital more than at home.
there are significant differences in end-of life decision making across countries and across care settings within countries.
there is no single best place for dying.
